newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African fishing firms told to help blacks.
newsitem.headline: South African fishing firms told to help blacks.

text.p: South Africa's minister in charge of sea fisheries, Pallo Jordan, issued a veiled warning to industry majors on Thursday to promote black participation.

Jordan, minister of tourism and the environment, told a news conference that he planned to scrap the present quota board and replace it with a state-owned company which would allocate "access rights" to marine resources.
"The new policy will favour small to medium-sized enterprises and...provide incentives to major fishing corporations to restructure their ownership and achieve empowerment objectives," he said.
Asked if he would take a carrot and stick approach to achieve black empowerment, Jordan said:
"We reserve the stick at this point in time. The responsiveness of industry will determine whether it ever has to be unsheathed or not."
He said the attitude of companies would be taken into account when access rights were allocated.
"If you have to choose between people who want to live in the old South Africa, and those who want to live in the new, you will tend to favour those who are committed to the new," Jordan said.
"We cannot have a situation where the disparities of the past just continue in a business as usual fashion," Jordan said.
He said the companies that dominated the industry now, like Irvin&Johnson, Sea Harvest Corp and Oceana Fishing Group, had benefited from apartheid policies which kept blacks out of boardrooms.
"Given the history of racial exclusion...(blacks) are keenly aware that the big companies that dominate the sector today owe their position not solely to merit," Jordan said.
But he said he was reluctant to introduce policies that would harm these companies because they were the only internationally competitive players in the industry, and they provided thousands of jobs.
Some of the companies had already started empowerment programmes, Jordan said.
